name: User Control and Freedom
description: Users should be able to back out, undo, cancel, or leave unwanted states without feeling trapped. Recoverability matters as much as initial correctness.
design_relevance_note: Shows up in destructive actions, modal flows, onboarding skip paths, filters, navigation dead-ends, undo toasts, draft-saving, and any flow where people need a safe exit.
myth_risk_note: Updated 2026-09-07: myth risk raised from unset/low to moderate. The one real empirical test found actively complicates the popular 'always give users control' reading of this heuristic (in a health-behavior-website context, less control produced more engagement and learning) -- exactly the gap between confident popular usage and what evidence actually shows that myth_risk exists to flag.
prevalence_note: A core Nielsen heuristic and one of the most common UI-review checks, especially for forms, destructive actions, modals, and navigation flows.

findings.description: In a randomized 3-arm trial of a hepatitis-education website, giving users LESS control (a tunneled, forced-sequence version) produced lower perceived efficiency but significantly more pages visited, more time on site, and more knowledge gained a week later, compared to a high-choice version letting users skip pages freely -- directly contradicting the popular framing of Nielsen's "user control and freedom" heuristic as straightforwardly beneficial. The tunneled version also drove higher overall website use than the free-choice version.
findings.effect_size: F(1,452)=97.69 (perceived efficiency, P<.001); F(1,452)=171.49 (pages visited, P<.001); F(1,452)=6.32 (time on site, P=.01); F(1,452)=134.32 (knowledge gained, P<.001) -- all favoring the tunneled (less-control) version except perceived efficiency
findings.source_title: The Role of User Control in Adherence to and Knowledge Gained from a Website: Randomized Comparison Between a Tunneled Version and a Freedom-of-Choice Version

applications.title: Delta app's 'Back' link that actually cancels the flight search
applications.description: In Delta's mobile app, once a user selects a flight, tapping 'Back' does not return them to the flight list as expected -- it functions as a full cancel, forcing the user to redo the entire search from scratch. NN/g's usability observation of this flow argues the mislabeled control likely discourages users from comparing alternative flights before booking.
applications.ethical_note: It is genuinely unclear whether Delta's Back-as-Cancel behavior is a deliberate friction pattern discouraging users from abandoning a flight selection to compare alternatives, or simply an engineering oversight where the button's actual behavior was never aligned with its label. NN/g's own framing treats it as an incidental usability defect rather than a named dark pattern, and no source confirms intent either way, so unclear is the honest grade rather than assuming malice or innocence.
